newsitem.title: USA: Stars arrive for glittering Oscar ceremony.
newsitem.headline: Stars arrive for glittering Oscar ceremony.

text.p: The stars, the directors and the producers arrived at the Shrine Auditorium on Monday night for Hollywood's biggest extravaganza of the year -- the Academy Awards.

But while the shining limousines lined up outside the auditorium with their valuable cargoes of celebrities, Hollywood power brokers and Oscar nominees hoping for a glittering, glitch-free evening, there was already trouble in the skies.

One small aircraft circling above the Shrine trailed a banner reading, "Columbia Studios Sucks -- Larry Flynt," in an apparent reference to the fact that the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, which presents the awards, had deliberately not invited the controversial publisher of "Hustler" magazine to join in the ceremony, despite the fact that Woody Harrelson's portrayal of him in the film, "The People vs. Larry Flynt" garnered a best actor Oscar nomination for the former "Cheers" star of television.
Walt Disney Studios also came under an aerial bombardment over its alleged sweatshop practices in Haiti, where some of Disney's clothing and memorablia lines are manufactured.
"Disney uses sweatshops -- 30 cents an hour in Haiti," a skyborne banner read.
On another political note, the Rev. Jesse Jackson railed against racism in Hollywood ahead of the Oscars, a year after the civil rights activist picketed the event.

"Today there are still too few people of colour being hired as writers, directors, and producers," Jackson said. "It would seem the aspirations of blacks, Latinos and others have hit perpetual yield signs and in most cases have been held up at red lights throughout this lucrative industry."
Meanwhile, nothing could spoil the pleasure of thousands of movie fans who gathered outside the auditorium to watch their favourite stars arrive.

They reserved their loudest cheers not for a movie personality but for boxing great Muhammad Ali as he walked up the red carpet. Ali was at the Oscars for the documentary "When We Were Kings," a film about his famous 1974 prize fight with George Foreman in Zaire.
Legions of fans, some of whom had been outside since Thursday, were armed with cameras, hoping to snap a picture of their favourite stars.
"I slept on the concrete," Kenan Jones, who had camped out for two nights, said. "It hurt bad, but it was worth it."
Other hardy fans had been camping in the temporary stands since they were erected on Thursday.

The Shrine Auditorium was a hub of activity early on Monday as carpenters hammered the final nails into the stage and scenery and electricians adjusted the 450 computer-controlled moving spotlights for the night when Hollywood outdoes itself with extravagance.

This is the night the movie-making capital of the world puts on a show. Part of the glitter will come from $140 million worth of diamonds donated by an international jeweller and destined for the necks, wrists and earlobes of the famous -- if only for Oscar night.
In addition, the world's most famous fashion designers have been knocking each other over to entice the stars to wear their gowns and tuxedos.
After the show, it's party time as studios hope to attract the rich and famous to their post-Oscar bashes.

Apart from the traditional "Governor's Ball" for 1,650 guests, Elton John's AIDS benefit party was expected to be the hottest ticket in town. The all-star guests will also have the chance to sing "Happy Birthday" to the singer, who turns 50 the following day.

This year, apart from Hollywood legend Lauren Bacall ("The Mirror Has Two Faces") in the best supporting actress category, there were no obvious favourites to grab the Oscars handed out by the Academy.

"The English Patient," which picked up the most nominations with 12, was thought to have a chance of winning for best picture, but is up against a Tom Cruise blockbuster, "Jerry Maguire," and three quirky independently produced films, "Secrets & Lies," "Shine" and "Fargo."
Lead actors Ralph Fiennes and Kristin Scott Thomas and "The English Patient" director Anthony Minghella were nominated, along with Juliette Binoche, as best supporting actress.
Cruise and Fiennes were joined in the best actor category by Woody Harrelson for "The People vs. Larry Flynt," Geoffrey Rush for "Shine" and Billy Bob Thornton for "Sling Blade."
Along with Scott Thomas, the best actress nominees were Brenda Blethyn ("Secrets & Lies"), Frances McDormand ("Fargo"), Emily Watson ("Breaking the Waves") and Diane Keaton ("Marvin's Room").
